title: Tech stocks are plunging. Is it a buying opportunity or a falling knife?
excerpt: It's been the roughest week for the tech trade since Liberation Day. We asked investors whether it's time to buy at better prices or to sit back.
content_html:
The AI sell-off has investors on edge. 5 pros weigh in on whether to buy the dip — or skip.

By Alex Nicoll

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T11:01:01.275Z

Hopes that Anthropic's IPO would reverse the post-election tech sell-off have been dashed. Now, investors are increasingly concerned that the AI trade will be the next thing to deflate — or that maybe it already has.

The Nasdaq has now slipped into negative territory for 2026, and has had its worst week in well over a year. The sell-off following a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections and growing anti-data-center sentiment was then compounded by the fallout from Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's resignation and concerns about the chip industry's ties to China.

And while Anthropic hit the public markets at a staggering 34% above its IPO price, it nearly dropped back to its debut pricing of $83 per share around Friday at noon.

There's a long-standing cliché that investors should buy the dip. Markets go up over time, after all, though there's always the possibility that some AI supercomputer decides to destroy humanity and all of its shareholder value.

But buying at the wrong time can leave an investor underwater for many years.

It's the battle of the dueling investment clichés: is it time to buy the dip? Or would that be catching a falling knife?

Business Insider spoke to five investors who see opportunities emerging from the sell-off, even as some warn that the worst could still be ahead. Their advice: be selective, pay attention to valuations, and not buy blindly.

A bit of both

Dan Niles, semiconductor investor and founder of Niles Investment Management, told Business Insider that we could very well be seeing a substantial stock correction, but that doesn't mean there isn't money to be made.

"The world changed on November 3rd," he said, noting that the Blue Wave and a near sweep of local ballot initiatives that slow or ban data center development have already spooked the market.

And now, new legislators will take office in January right before companies provide earnings guidance for the coming quarter. Niles thinks companies will give worse-than-expected guidance amid changing political winds, which could further weigh on the market.

There may be more market peaks ahead, Niles said, but we could also be in a "horrific downdraft," akin to the market turmoil of 1997 and 1998 that preceded the March 2000 peak.

In the two and a half years after the dot-com bubble burst, the semiconductor sector rallied seven times, averaging 28% each rally, while losing 83% in total, he said.

In today's market, he's choosing to look at fundamentals. He told Business Insider earlier this week that he's taking a long position in Nvidia and doesn't think we've seen the top of the chip market yet.

He's taking long positions in South Korean semiconductor firms that have been battered by volatility in the Korean stock market. Names like Samsung and SK Hynix trade at three to four times future earnings, while Anthropic is trading at 20 times its projected revenue for the year, he said.

"If you like the AI trade, to me, those two things are very different," he told CNBC on Friday.

Fear might be worse than the fundamentals

It's notoriously difficult to pick the bottom, says Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, but the level of fear in the market and tech sell-off are signs that things could move in the other direction soon. They just haven't yet.

"The consistency of selling is frustrating dip buyers," he said. He sees similarities with other short-term downturns earlier this year and last year, which were driven more by fear than actual changes in the economy.

This should be a sign to buy, "but emotional investors can overwhelm opportunistic ones in the short term," he said.

Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, agreed that it's a buying opportunity. He suggested dollar-cost averaging, the practice of investing a certain dollar amount regularly, because his firm doesn't anticipate a simple V-shaped recovery.

He said Wells is neutral on tech investments, so they wouldn't recommend increasing exposure to that sector; instead, it prefers to put money in US large-cap stocks in the communication services, industrials, and materials sectors.

There just aren't any real economic changes like a recession or negative earnings growth that cause lasting market downturns, he said.

"The developments that would lead us to believe the trend is changing are not currently in place, which is why even if the knife keeps falling it would represent an opportunity for intermediate- to long-term investors," he said.

Bob Shea, chief investment officer at Dynasty Financial Partners, also sees the opportunity for long-term investors to get in at "compelling" prices, while short-term investors sell off.

"The amount of money focused on short-term profits has grown enormously since 2020," Shea said, citing the growth in trading from large hedge funds and retail, "armed with single-day expiry options and 2x and 3x levered ETFs."

That money has "tight leashes," and it's now hitting its risk limits and getting out, he said, citing major hedge fund blowups like Situational Awareness.

"Right now everyone is pricing in an AI bust, and I'm pressing on my thesis, asking what can go right here," he said. That doesn't mean buying indiscriminately. Shea favors active managers over an index, "which is a sitting duck if a company quickly becomes irrelevant."

Michael McGowan, chief investment strategist at $110 billion wealth manager Pathstone, agrees that this sell-off is a "healthy cooling" of market exuberance. His firm is now selectively adding exposure to hardware and mega-cap companies after being underweight for most of the year.

There's going to be "dispersion" between companies that can build their own data centers and those that rely on debt and outside capital, he said, but he's seeing value in tech again.

"Tech now trades at a lower forward multiple than the broader S&P for the first time since before the pandemic, even as cloud revenue growth at the hyperscalers has accelerated," he said.

The sell-off following a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections and growing anti-data-center sentiment was then compounded by the fallout from Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's resignation and concerns about the chip industry's ties to China.

And while Anthropic hit the public markets at a staggering 34% above its IPO price, it nearly dropped back to its debut pricing of $83 per share around Friday at noon.

There's a long-standing cliché that investors should buy the dip. Markets go up over time, after all, though there's always the possibility that some AI supercomputer decides to destroy humanity and all of its shareholder value.

But buying at the wrong time can leave an investor underwater for many years.

It's the battle of the dueling investment clichés: is it time to buy the dip? Or would that be catching a falling knife?

Business Insider spoke to five investors who see opportunities emerging from the sell-off, even as some warn that the worst could still be ahead. Their advice: be selective, pay attention to valuations, and not buy blindly.

A bit of both

Dan Niles, semiconductor investor and founder of Niles Investment Management, told Business Insider that we could very well be seeing a substantial stock correction, but that doesn't mean there isn't money to be made.

"The world changed on November 3rd," he said, noting that the Blue Wave and a near sweep of local ballot initiatives that slow or ban data center development have already spooked the market.

And now, new legislators will take office in January right before companies provide earnings guidance for the coming quarter. Niles thinks companies will give worse-than-expected guidance amid changing political winds, which could further weigh on the market.

There may be more market peaks ahead, Niles said, but we could also be in a "horrific downdraft," akin to the market turmoil of 1997 and 1998 that preceded the March 2000 peak.

In the two and a half years after the dot-com bubble burst, the semiconductor sector rallied seven times, averaging 28% each rally, while losing 83% in total, he said.

In today's market, he's choosing to look at fundamentals. He told Business Insider earlier this week that he's taking a long position in Nvidia and doesn't think we've seen the top of the chip market yet.

He's taking long positions in South Korean semiconductor firms that have been battered by volatility in the Korean stock market. Names like Samsung and SK Hynix trade at three to four times future earnings, while Anthropic is trading at 20 times its projected revenue for the year, he said.

"If you like the AI trade, to me, those two things are very different," he told CNBC on Friday.

Fear might be worse than the fundamentals

It's notoriously difficult to pick the bottom, says Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, but the level of fear in the market and tech sell-off are signs that things could move in the other direction soon. They just haven't yet.

"The consistency of selling is frustrating dip buyers," he said. He sees similarities with other short-term downturns earlier this year and last year, which were driven more by fear than actual changes in the economy.

This should be a sign to buy, "but emotional investors can overwhelm opportunistic ones in the short term," he said.

Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, agreed that it's a buying opportunity. He suggested dollar-cost averaging, the practice of investing a certain dollar amount regularly, because his firm doesn't anticipate a simple V-shaped recovery.

He said Wells is neutral on tech investments, so they wouldn't recommend increasing exposure to that sector; instead, it prefers to put money in US large-cap stocks in the communication services, industrials, and materials sectors.

There just aren't any real economic changes like a recession or negative earnings growth that cause lasting market downturns, he said.

"The developments that would lead us to believe the trend is changing are not currently in place, which is why even if the knife keeps falling it would represent an opportunity for intermediate- to long-term investors," he said.

Bob Shea, chief investment officer at Dynasty Financial Partners, also sees the opportunity for long-term investors to get in at "compelling" prices, while short-term investors sell off.

"The amount of money focused on short-term profits has grown enormously since 2020," Shea said, citing the growth in trading from large hedge funds and retail, "armed with single-day expiry options and 2x and 3x levered ETFs."

That money has "tight leashes," and it's now hitting its risk limits and getting out, he said, citing major hedge fund blowups like Situational Awareness.

"Right now everyone is pricing in an AI bust, and I'm pressing on my thesis, asking what can go right here," he said. That doesn't mean buying indiscriminately. Shea favors active managers over an index, "which is a sitting duck if a company quickly becomes irrelevant."

Michael McGowan, chief investment strategist at $110 billion wealth manager Pathstone, agrees that this sell-off is a "healthy cooling" of market exuberance. His firm is now selectively adding exposure to hardware and mega-cap companies after being underweight for most of the year.

There's going to be "dispersion" between companies that can build their own data centers and those that rely on debt and outside capital, he said, but he's seeing value in tech again.

"Tech now trades at a lower forward multiple than the broader S&P for the first time since before the pandemic, even as cloud revenue growth at the hyperscalers has accelerated," he said.
